articles.text: Fire destroyed Galloway Bros. livery stable in Mandan, Tuesday evening. The loss is about $1,500. Insurance, $250.
articles.summary: Fire destroys Galloway Bros. livery stable at Mandan; loss about $1,500.

articles.text: The ice palace in St. Paul will be completed by Feb. 1. Grand preparations are being made for the opening carnival and reduced rates will be quoted on all roads.
articles.summary: St. Paul ice palace to be finished by Feb. 1 with reduced rail rates for the carnival.

articles.text: All through the east, snow blockades have been the rule for the past week or two. The Northern Pacific has not had a serious blockade this winter, the greatest delay being only a few hours.
articles.summary: Snow blockades in the east; the Northern Pacific has had no serious blockade this winter.

articles.text: Judge Moody, senator elect from the would-be state of Dakota, has been accorded the privilege of admission to the floor of the Senate. Its dollars to doughnuts his state (?) will get no farther than this recognition.
articles.summary: Judge Moody, senator-elect of the would-be state of Dakota, admitted to the Senate floor; the paper doubts statehood will go further.

articles.text: Glowing reports of a new gold field in Honduras are published. Col. Pat. Donan is one of the syndicate who seem ta be advertising the matter, however, and the account is very liable to be flowery.
articles.summary: Skeptical note on reported Honduras gold field promoted by a syndicate including Col. Pat. Donan.

articles.text: The statehood movement has made no progress except that advocates of all manners of division and admission as a whole have ventilated their opinions before the House commitee on Territories. We see no reason to change our opinion that either Dakota will be admitted as a whole or that nothing whatever will be accomplished.
articles.summary: Statehood movement makes no progress; the paper expects Dakota admitted whole or nothing.

articles.text: There seems but little doubt that the county will soon be organized. It is utterly impossible that the wish of over 170 citizens can longer be thwarted, especially when there were only two citizens who refused to sign the petition for organization. It is high time the call was issued, so that immediate steps can be taken toward fighting the law under which Stark county is attempting to tax us. It will be well-nigh impossible for individuals to fight this law separately but as a county we can fight it well and we think successfully.
articles.summary: Organization of Billings county expected soon, after 170 citizens petitioned; aim is to fight Stark county taxation.

articles.text: Reports from Missouri, Kansas and Nebraska show a terrible loss on cattle owing to the late blizzard. The universal tendency of reporters with reference to cattle losses and we might add, with reference to all cattle interests, is to grossly exaggerate the facts. The losses referred to are too well established to admit of doubt. While stockmen in Dakota and Montana are congratulating themselves the southern stockmen are counting losses. "Their gains are not."
articles.summary: Heavy cattle losses from the blizzard in Missouri, Kansas and Nebraska, while Dakota and Montana stockmen fare well.

articles.text: A good deal of quiet work is being done toward opening up the Crow reservation in Montana. If we mistake not there are nearly 5,000,000 acres in the reservation occupied by about 500 families of Crows. As the game is practically gone, at least three-quarters of this valuable land is utterly useless to the Crows and they could make it much more profitable by getting Congress to increase their rations by relinquishing the greater part of the reservation. Exactly a parallel case is the great Sioux reservation of Dakota. We hope, and have good reason to believe, that this reservation will be opened this winter if Congress can stop quarrelling long enough to attend to it.
articles.summary: Argues for opening the Crow reservation in Montana and the great Sioux reservation of Dakota.

articles.text: A number of persons to whom we have spoken, do not intend paying their taxes to Stark county. Except for the five per cent. penalty, in case the law authorizing the tax is declared constitutional, the more who refuse, the better. We believe the law can be declared unconstitutional, and in that event, those refusing to pay taxes will be gainers in the use of their money from the time they would have paid, to the time in which they recovered them. The only real and substantial reason for paying taxes under this law, is to avoid a possible five per cent. penalty. As far as we personally are concerned, we do not intend paying our taxes to Stark county until compelled to do so. Our reason for this is solely our belief in the unconstitutionality of the law. As we have said in this and former issues, the only reason for paying at all, is to avoid a possible five per cent penalty.
articles.summary: Packard says he and others will not pay taxes to Stark county, believing the law unconstitutional.

articles.text: Although crowded ranges in the Bad Lands have in a few instances made the cattle scatter badly, in search of food, the vast majority of stock is and has been doing well. It is the general remark that this is the lightest winter we have yet had on stock in the Bad Lands.
articles.summary: The Bad Lands winter is called the lightest yet on stock, though crowded ranges scatter some cattle.

articles.text: There is a big scheme on foot to establish a grand system of dressed meat refrigerators at San Antonio, with a line of steamers to aid the Aransas Pass road in getting it to market. The Aransas Pass road has a finger in the scheme and it will sooner or later be a go. Get the beef and mutton ready.—[Texas Stockman.
articles.summary: Scheme for dressed-meat refrigerators at San Antonio with Aransas Pass road (from Texas Stockman).

articles.text: All over the range country, from the Canadian Pacific to the Gulf of Mexico, come rumors of the establishment in the near future, of large slaughter-houses. Texas will be forced to adopt the plan and the increased profit in cattle sold as dressed beef, will draw many others into the plan. It requires no prophet to foretell that this will soon become the popular method of marketing range beef.
articles.summary: Rumors across the range country of large slaughter-houses; dressed beef expected to become the popular method.

articles.text: The Marquis de Mores, the Dakota cattle king, was among the passengers on the steamer Labrador, which arrived from Havre this morning. In answer to questions, the Marquis said he had a splendid trip and received a warm welcome in France. He thinks the prospects of the cattle business are very good, especially between France and America. He intends to make the experiment of exporting young cattle and taking them to France for feeding and breeding purposes and expresses himself as confident of success.—[Inter Ocean, Jan. 21.
articles.summary: Inter Ocean reports the Marquis de Mores arrived from Havre on the Labrador and plans to export young cattle to France.

articles.text: A. Osborne of the Ætna ranch, was in town Tuesday. His "black doddies" are doing well and he is an enthusiastic champion of black blood. He advocates a plan that is novel enough to be striking and the more we think about it, the more its good points, at least in a modified form, impress themselves upon us. His plan is to have a mid-winter calf round-up and take the calves and if necessary, their mothers, to different ranches, to be cared for. It is an indisputable fact that although the most of the cattle are in fine condition, the winter calves and their mothers are now and in fact, every winter, are in bad fix. We have on the one hand, a saving of a five per cent. and upward yearly loss on calves born in winter and their mothers, a material lessening of the range cattleman's greatest source of loss. On the other hand, we have the impossibility of rounding-up in some of the coldest weather, the harm arising from "ginning up" cattle in winter, the increased cost in feeding and caring for the animals taken up, the great danger of accidents in riding or driving over rough and frozen ground and many other objections that will readily occur to anyone who thinks over the matter. Will the returns justify the out-lay? If the recent cold snap is really broken and our winter continues as mild as it has been, the answer must be in the negative. If cattle should enter on a hard winter in poor condition, it certainly would pay. But right here, as we are met by the almost total impossibility of rounding-up in severe weather, the question remains as far from solution as ever. There is no question, however, that it would pay to ride the ranges more constantly than is now done and in case a cow and calf need help and are not too far from the ranch, they can be driven there and cared for. We have seen many cows with calves this winter on the range, which were near their owners' home ranches and which would have been greatly benefitted and in several cases have had their lives saved, by being cared for. The calf round-up could certainly be worked profitably to this extent.
articles.summary: A. Osborne of the Aetna ranch, in town Tuesday, praises his black doddies and proposes a mid-winter calf round-up; the paper weighs the idea.

articles.headline: Breaking Bronchos.
articles.text:
Some time last year the Journal kindly permitted me space for a little article under the above caption.

Since then I have witnessed some successful "broncho busters" handle a lot of unbroken colts, and I will endeavor simply to describe what I saw.

The band of horses which they were breaking are well proportioned, active, and about the average weight and size, universally admitted to be the finest, most carefully selected lot of western saddle horses ever unloaded at Miles. Among them are the usual proportion of "hard buckers" and vicious ones found in every band of horses.

There were two "busters," each having a "helper."

Two bronchos were quietly cut out and left in a moderately close corral, one for each breaker. A broncho was roped (on foot) by the front feet and thrown. Instantly a "leading rope" was put on. This consisted simply of a small rope about 30 feet long, having at one end a loop about 7 or 8 inches long. This loop was forced into the broncho's mouth, so that it was at once a sort of rope bit and curb. Then the long end of the rope was passed over the head and through the off side of the loop; then it was brought over the head back again and through the near side of the loop, making a sort of headstall.

This done, the broncho was permitted to rise and run around the corral at will till he became perfectly used to the trailing rope and entirely indiffernt to it.

Then came the first lesson. The breaker approached the rope quietly, picked it up, and if the broncho started to move off, gave the rope a strong pull (not jerk) to teach it that it could not escape, and that the loop would hurt its mouth every time it tried to pull loose.

In a few moments the breaker could approach the broncho at will and pet and caress it. It was no longer afraid of him, and stood always head toward him.

Very slowly he pulled it around, first to the right then to the left, only a step or two at a time. Again as soon as the broncho knew what was wanted it made this move quickly. Then it was led forward slowly a few steps at a time. Again, as soon as it knew what was wanted, the broncho led up. In a very little while it would lead easily and quickly anywhere.

Then a lariat loop was reeved around its middle and the lariat given sharp jerks. This made the broncho buck in every instance, but the jerking was continued till the broncho no longer bucked. It was then let run at will with the rope around its middle and dragging against its legs till the broncho had examined it by smelling at it and was entirely indifferent to it.

The saddle and saddle cloth were then passed to it and it was permitted to smell at and examine both until it learned there was nothing in either to hurt it. Then slowly and quietly the saddle was placed on its back and latigoes reeved. Then quickly and quietly the cinches were tightened and buckled. In some cases the blind was necessary to do this, but in most, not. Then the broncho was given its liberty to run around the corral. If it was quiet, the saddle was soon removed. If it bucked it was permitted to run and buck around the corral till it quit bucking, quieted down and seemed perfectly indifferent and careless about the saddle.

Then a doubled rope was fastened by the middle to the saddle horn and the ends permitted to drag, one under each hind leg and flank. Again the broncho was let have the freedom of the corral until it found these ropes would not hurt it and cared nothing for their dragging over its flanks and between its hind legs.

The broncho was then unsaddled and unhaltered and let to stand to hay in the corral all the afternoon. Next morning it was ridden either with hackamore or bit, in the usual way for colts. The majority moved off quietly without running or bucking a single lick, and in no instance was a blind required in mounting.

At each obedience the broncho was petted and caressed. It was never scolded or struck angrily. Perfect quiet was preserved around the corral.

Before freeing from the "leading rope," some of the bronchos were made to stand perfectly quiet while a lariat was swung under their noses or flung at will over their heads, and they were so afraid of that jaw loop that they trembled violently, but dared not move.

After being ridden once or twice, the horses broken in the above manner have proved gentle and quiet, do not buck, and are not afraid of a rope dragging between their hind legs.

We do not know if the above is a "system," but we commend the method, for we saw it worked successfully, and we gamble on success every time, you bet.—[Pony Bill in Stockgrowers' Journal.
articles.summary: Reprinted letter by 'Pony Bill' (Stockgrowers' Journal) describing a gentle method of breaking bronchos seen at Miles.

articles.headline: Cattle Brands.
articles.text:
The young maverick savant could take a [kindergargarten?] course in the study of cow-brands. Here a wide field opens up to the scholar. The adult steer in the great realm of beef is now a walking Chinese wash-bill, a Hindoo poem in the original junk-shop alphabet, a four-legged Greek inscription punctuated with jim-jams, a stenographer's notes of a riot, a bird's eye view of a premature explosion in a hardware store.

The cowboy who can at once grapple with the great problem of where to put the steer with "B bar B" on left shoulder, "Key Circle G" on left side, "Heart [illegible] Heart" on right hip, left ear crop, wattle wattle, and seven hands round, with "Dash B Dash" on right shoulder "vented," wattle on dewlap "vented," and "[illegible] D Q," "C O D" and "N G" vented on right side, keeping track of transfers, range and postoffice of last owner, has certainly got a future which lies mostly ahead of him.

Perhaps I have said too much on this subject, but when I get thoroughly awakened on this great porter-house steak problem, I am apt to carry the matter too far.—[Bill Nye.
articles.summary: Bill Nye's humorous piece on the complexity of cattle brands (reprint).

articles.summary: Pat. O'Hara goes to Helena.

articles.text: Mrs. Wm. Paddock is expected back this evening.
articles.summary: Mrs. Wm. Paddock expected back this evening.

articles.text: The river raised about six inches yesterday, the water flowing over the ice.
articles.summary: Little Missouri rose about six inches over the ice.

articles.text: Fred Willard started for Deadwood Tuesday morning. He will go in by way of Chadron.
articles.summary: Fred Willard leaves for Deadwood via Chadron.

articles.text: Howard Eaton came up from his ranch Monday and reported everything lovely on the VI range.
articles.summary: Howard Eaton reports all well on the VI range.

articles.text: N. A. Thayer and his bridge crew are here repairing the bridge which was drawn out of shape by the cold weather.
articles.summary: N. A. Thayer's crew repairing the railroad bridge warped by cold.

articles.text: The ice contract of Frank Foster with the N. P. R. R. was thrown up, owing to the difficulty of keeping a locomotive here to do the necessary switching.
articles.summary: Frank Foster's N.P. ice contract given up over switching difficulties.

articles.text: F. I. Ellison of Mandan, came in from the east Friday evening and after a brief visit with his brother, C. F. returned Saturday morning.
articles.summary: F. I. Ellison of Mandan visits his brother C. F. Ellison.

articles.text: J. C. Fisher is getting to be such an expert polishing horns that admiring friends are said to pay fabulous prices for his work and to place them on exhibition as souvenirs.
articles.summary: J. C. Fisher's polished horns are prized as souvenirs.

articles.text: Mr. and Mrs. J. N. Maxwell are now living in St. Paul. Mr. Maxwell takes a position as messenger for the Wells-Fargo, with a run between St. Paul and Fargo.
articles.summary: J. N. Maxwell, now of St. Paul, becomes a Wells-Fargo messenger.

articles.text: Geo. A. Cole returned Saturday night from St. Paul, where he closed the office of the N. P. Ref. Car Co. The headquarters of the company will hereafter be in Medora.
articles.summary: Geo. A. Cole closes the N. P. Refrigerator Car Co. St. Paul office; headquarters now Medora.

articles.text: W. D. Williams, who has been here for some time looking up a chance to invest in stock, left for the east last Sunday morning. The weather was too cold for him to look around much during his stay and he expects to return.
articles.summary: W. D. Williams, prospective cattle investor, leaves for the east.

articles.text: Supt. Green was in Medora Tuesday morning. He has sent his family to Puget sound for the winter and will go for them in the spring. His duties on the Missouri division have prevented him from ever going west of Glendive personally.
articles.summary: Supt. Green in Medora; family wintering on Puget Sound.

articles.text: Chas. Cook has started a drug store in the Red Mountain mining district north of Helena. The Helena Herald is a strong advocate of a railroad from Helena to Rimini, the supply point of the district and the place where the "four-eyed blonde" is now in business.
articles.summary: Former Medora man Chas. Cook opens a drug store in the Red Mountain district near Helena.

articles.text: Willis Eaton and Harry Tarbell came down from the Logging camp and Horse ranch yesterday. They report seeing only one dead animal so far and that a through Texan of last year's drive, but that the recent cold snap had a very weakening effect on the cattle.
articles.summary: Willis Eaton and Harry Tarbell report few cattle losses but weakening from the cold snap.

articles.text: Charley C. Conley, well known to Montana and Dakota cowmen, died Jan. 9. at the Hot Springs, Arkansas. He had formerly been an inspector for the Wyoming stock association and of late years worked for the Hashknife and E6 outfits. He leaves a widow in the Black Hills.
articles.summary: Death of cowman Charley C. Conley at Hot Springs, Ark.

articles.text: W. H. Merrifield and "Sylvane" Ferris started for Chicago last Friday morning on receipt of a telegram from Theodore Roosevelt inviting them to meet him there. The boys anticipated a first-rate time and are probably now enjoying it. "Sylvane" will return in a few days but Merrifield will make a longer stay "in and about" St. Paul.
articles.summary: Merrifield and Sylvane Ferris go to Chicago at Theodore Roosevelt's invitation.

articles.text: Again has there come a time for congratulation. Some time yesterday in New Brunswick, Joe. Ferris was made happy by taking unto himself a better half. We must postpone the publication of particulars or draw on our imagination, so we can only wish the newly married couple all manner of prosperity. They will probably return the last of February.
articles.summary: Joe Ferris married in New Brunswick.

articles.text: W. Aug. Fonda is being shown up in good shape by the Mandan Pioneer. In some mysterious way he was appointed post-master at Stanton to replace a lady whom every one liked. W. Aug. left a very unsavory reputation here but by all who knew him, was excused on account of a supposed mental weakness. Go to him, Bro. Tuttle.
articles.summary: W. Aug. Fonda's appointment as Stanton postmaster criticized.

articles.text: A chinook came down on us in full force yesterday and the snow began to disappear rapidly. Last night the thermometer went down again, forming a slight crust on the snow. To-day, the weather is milder, being 12 above at twelve o'clock. The recent cold snap humped the cattle up considerably and they will need some warm weather in which to recuperate.
articles.summary: Chinook melts snow; cattle need warm weather after the cold snap.

articles.text: We wish to call especial attention to our offer of Huffman's round-up views. They consist of thirty-six handsomely finished photographs of the most prominent round-up scenes and are well worth double $5 for which they invariably have and will be sold. To subscribers, however, we offer the complete set and the Cow Boy for a year for $6 cash. This is really getting the paper for $1 a year, as the views have not and will not be sold for less than $5. Call at our office and examine the photographs.
articles.summary: Cow Boy promotes Huffman's round-up photographs premium.
